terms.gloss: to set out to be seen, to put on show
evidence: Cic. Mur. 75: exposuit vāsa Samia (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: To set things out where they can be seen, in a house or in pūblicō. Its other common senses are to set forth in words, to explain, to land troops from ships, and to expose a child (Lewis & Short).
To set out in front, to display, as goods for sale (see display) or a notice in public; also to propose, to offer a prize, to set before the mind (Lewis & Short).
Cicero’s phrase for pictures and statues set out in a rich house; Morgan–Owens gives it for a museum’s exhibits.

terms.gloss: to produce, to present; to show
terms.comment: Mostly to hand over or produce a person or a document (as in court), to furnish, and to keep, maintain; “show, display” is a rarer, chiefly poetic sense (Lewis & Short). Not the plain word for exhibiting art.

phrases.latin: nōn explicātā veste neque prōpositō argentō neque tabulīs et signīs prōpalam conlocātīs
phrases.english: with no clothes unfolded, no silver set out, no pictures and statues put openly on show

phrases.latin: pingī autem … mūnera atque in pūblicō expōnī coepta ā C. Terentiō Lūcānō
phrases.english: the painting of [gladiatorial] shows and their exhibition in public began with Gaius Terentius Lucanus

sources: Lewis & Short: expono · Lewis & Short: propono · Lewis & Short: propalam · Lewis & Short: exhibeo
